question: Summarize key research papers that have empirically evaluated open-source 5G testbeds specifically designed for O-RAN?

sections.text: The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) paradigm promises a disaggregated, interoperable RAN with programmable control, but realizing this vision requires extensive experimentation on realistic platforms. Traditional cellular testbeds and vendor equipment often lack the flexibility or accessibility for open RAN research. As a result, researchers have turned to open-source 5G platforms and custom testbeds to evaluate O-RAN concepts in practice. However, existing platforms sometimes “lack the fidelity and stability” needed to explore advanced O-RAN use cases [7]. This has led to a surge of **open-source 5G O-RAN testbeds** – experimental networks that combine open software with O-RAN’s architecture – to enable empirical evaluation of performance, interoperability, and new control algorithms in 5G RANs.

sections.text: One key research theme is integrating O-RAN’s *RAN Intelligent Controller* (RIC) with open-source RAN implementations. Upadhyaya *et al.* (2022) demonstrated how to build a software-defined radio (SDR) 5G testbed that connects an open-source 5G standalone (SA) RAN stack to O-RAN’s near-real-time RIC via standard interfaces [2]. In their prototype, a 5G gNB (base station) based on open software was made O-RAN compliant by enabling the O-RAN E2 interface and an E2 agent. They successfully ran two custom **xApps** on the RIC that exchanged O-RAN E2 messages with the RAN, actively controlling RAN behavior in real time [2]. This showed that open 5G software (e.g., OpenAirInterface or srsRAN) can be extended to support the O-RAN architecture, allowing external intelligent controllers to tweak RAN parameters dynamically. Similarly, Yoo and Hong (2024) built an **open-source O-RAN testbed** and *thoroughly analyzed the open interface messages* (E2, O1, etc.) during operation [3]. They also implemented a sample xApp to demonstrate an end-to-end O-RAN use case on their testbed [3]. These efforts provide blueprints for academia and industry to set up O-RAN compliant 5G networks at low cost, using commodity hardware and open software while still supporting the new O-RAN control interfaces.

sections.text: Another line of research has focused on pushing open-source O-RAN performance toward commercial levels by leveraging heterogeneous hardware and software. An exemplar is the **X5G testbed** by Villa *et al.* (2024), which deployed an end-to-end O-RAN-compliant 5G network using a blend of open-source and industry-grade components. The X5G platform consists of **eight 5G base stations (gNBs)** integrating NVIDIA’s Aerial SDK for a GPU-accelerated 5G PHY, the open-source OpenAirInterface (OAI) stack for higher protocol layers, and an O-RAN Software Community near-RT RIC for closed-loop control [1]. The OAI gNBs interface with the NVIDIA PHY via the Small Cell Forum FAPI, and each gNB runs an E2 agent to communicate with the centralized RIC [1]. This multi-vendor setup was **empirically evaluated** using both real smartphones and emulated UEs. Notably, the X5G testbed achieved over **1.65 Gbps downlink** and 143 Mbps uplink cell throughput with 4 commercial smartphones per base station in over-the-air tests [1]. Such results are encouraging, as they demonstrate that an open-source RAN (OAI) augmented with hardware acceleration (GPU-based PHY) and guided by an O-RAN RIC can approach the performance of traditional proprietary RAN systems. The X5G experiments highlight that careful integration of open software with specialized hardware (and adherence to O-RAN interfaces) can yield a high-performance 5G O-RAN network in a real-world environment.

sections.text: Because O-RAN facilitates intelligent, software-defined control of the RAN, researchers have also developed testbed frameworks to design and evaluate **machine learning (ML) driven RAN control**. Bonati *et al.* (2023) introduced **OpenRAN Gym**, an open-source toolkit that provides a unified environment for **data collection, AI model training, and testing of O-RAN control applications** [4]. OpenRAN Gym is an O-RAN-compliant experimental toolbox that combines several software frameworks for gathering RAN statistics and for controlling the RAN via a lightweight near-RT RIC integrated into the testbed setup [4]. Using this toolkit, researchers can rapidly prototype new xApps (e.g. for radio resource management or interference mitigation) and evaluate them across heterogeneous platforms. For instance, OpenRAN Gym was used to deploy and test AI-driven xApps controlling a network of **7 base stations and 42 users** on the Colosseum wireless emulator [4]. In that experiment, the xApps were first trained and validated in a large-scale emulated RAN scenario (42 UE network), and then the same solutions were **ported to real-world testbeds** (including the Arena testbed and the POWDER and COSMOS platforms) with minimal changes [4]. This demonstrates how open-source O-RAN testbed frameworks can accelerate innovation: complex RAN control algorithms can be developed and tested at scale under realistic conditions, and later transferred to operational deployments. OpenRAN Gym’s contribution is thus in lowering the barrier for data-driven RAN research – providing an end-to-end pipeline from data collection to live testing – all aligned with O-RAN specifications.

sections.text: Complementing physical testbeds, the community has also created advanced **emulation platforms** serving as digital twins for O-RAN networks. A prime example is **Colosseum**, the world’s largest radio network emulator, which has been adapted to emulate O-RAN systems at scale. Polese *et al.* (2024) present Colosseum as an **“Open RAN Digital Twin”** – a high-fidelity environment where an entire 5G O-RAN network can be reproduced in software and tested before real deployment [5]. Colosseum includes a massive RF channel emulator (with 256 programmable SDRs) and supports end-to-end softwarized protocol stacks that are O-RAN and 5G compliant [5]. This allows researchers to instantiate virtual RAN nodes (O-CU/O-DU and RUs running open-source stacks like OAI or srsRAN) and have them interact over realistically emulated wireless channels. The platform can mimic large, complex scenarios – from city-wide cellular layouts to cross-technology interference – with full control and repeatability. Polese *et al.* showcase a broad range of **O-RAN use cases on Colosseum**, including real-time co-testing with a live network (connecting the emulator’s O-RAN nodes with an operational network in real time) and the development of ML-driven xApps under various radio conditions [5]. By acting as a digital twin, Colosseum enables rigorous experimentation and regression testing for O-RAN algorithms (such as RIC control policies) in a safe environment. This significantly accelerates research since new ideas can be vetted on Colosseum’s virtual yet realistic network before moving to physical testbeds. Overall, these emulation-based testbeds complement real-world open 5G testbeds by offering scale, controllability, and isolation (no risk to actual users) while still adhering to O-RAN architectures.

sections.text:
Empirical evaluation of open-source O-RAN is also happening in real-world deployments like private campuses and large-scale field testbeds. **Chepkoech *et al.*** (2023) describe a full **5G Standalone campus network** compliant with O-RAN, built using open-source software and commodity hardware. Their goal was to create a modular, low-cost and flexible 5G network for a university campus that avoids vendor lock-in. The deployed network leverages open architectures and software-defined networking concepts, using non-proprietary, programmable hardware in the RAN [8]. By using accessible open-source software (OSS) for every component, the campus network can be customized for specific performance needs (such as guaranteed bandwidth for certain applications, ultra-low latency, etc.) while significantly reducing costs [8]. The authors present this as a **“future-proof” 5G SA campus network** – one that can be easily adapted or upgraded via software updates and new xApps. This case study demonstrates the feasibility of rolling out O-RAN compliant 5G coverage in an enterprise or campus setting, and it provides practical insights (through the reported deployment and initial performance measurements) on what tuning might be required for reliability and quality of service in an open RAN.  

On an even larger scale, the **OpenRAN@Brasil** program (launched in 2024) is establishing a distributed O-RAN testbed spanning multiple sites across Brazil. The OpenRAN@Brasil testbed provides a specialized environment **reproducing real 5G network operating conditions**, where researchers and developers can safely **test and validate new components and functionalities** without affecting any commercial network traffic [9]. This open test platform invites academia and industry to experiment with O-RAN concepts (from rural coverage to advanced RIC applications) over a nationwide infrastructure. By offering a “safe space” for O-RAN experimentation [9], it lowers the barrier for validating innovative RAN ideas at scale. Although results are just beginning to emerge, this kind of large-scale open testbed will be key for examining how open RAN performs in wide-area, heterogeneous network scenarios (e.g., different regions, long backhaul links, multiple operators). It represents a significant step in translating open RAN research from isolated lab setups to distributed networks closer to real operator deployments.

sections.text: With many open-source O-RAN testbeds now available, researchers have started to compare their performance against traditional RAN systems to identify gaps. A notable study by Håkegård *et al.* (2024) evaluated a fully open-source O-RAN implementation (using the srsRAN stack) against both a closed-source O-RAN solution (a commercial Airspan system) and a proprietary 5G network. Their measurements revealed some performance disparities. For example, they found that **one-way packet delays and loss probabilities varied much more between different user devices** in the open-source O-RAN network (and in a legacy closed RAN) compared to the commercial O-RAN system [6]. In other words, the open-source O-RAN showed less consistent per-UE performance, whereas the vendor-optimized O-RAN tended to deliver more uniform quality of service across users [6]. These results provide a useful reality check: open-source RAN software, while extremely valuable for flexibility and innovation, may require further optimization to match the out-of-the-box stability of mature vendor solutions. The study by Håkegård *et al.* offers a **baseline for future improvements**, suggesting areas like scheduler efficiency and real-time processing where open implementations can be enhanced [6]. Complementary to this, other evaluations (e.g., the X5G testbed results) demonstrate that with targeted enhancements like hardware acceleration, open platforms **can** approach commercial performance. By synthesizing lessons from such empirical evaluations, the community can progressively refine open-source O-RAN platforms to improve their reliability, scalability and performance – accelerating their adoption in both research and operational networks.

question: How do AI/ML-based optimization techniques compare with traditional methods in terms of robustness, generalizability, and efficiency for end-to-end slice management under variable traffic and strict QoS requirements?

sections.text:
End-to-end network slicing is a key paradigm in 5G-and-beyond networks to meet diverse service requirements (e.g., enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency communications) under shared infrastructure. Slices come with heterogeneous QoS constraints – such as latency, throughput, and jitter – and must be allocated just enough resources to satisfy these strict QoS guarantees even as traffic loads fluctuate [3]. Achieving this is challenging because the relationship between allocated resources and QoS performance is complex and highly dynamic [3]. Traditionally, network slices have been managed via model-based optimizations or heuristic rules, but the increasing complexity (hundreds of configurable parameters per slice across multiple domains) makes purely manual or static solutions impractical [1]. This has led to growing interest in AI/ML-driven optimization techniques, which promise more adaptive and automated slice management. 

This report compares AI/ML-based optimization techniques with traditional methods for end-to-end slice management, focusing on **robustness** (ability to maintain performance under variable traffic), **generalizability** (applicability across scenarios beyond those explicitly tuned for), and **efficiency** (both in resource utilization and computational scalability). We survey a broad range of recent research, including surveys and case studies, and group findings into thematic categories. Contradictory results in the literature are discussed and reconciled to provide a balanced perspective.

sections.text:
Traditional slice management approaches typically rely on analytical modeling and optimization or fixed heuristics. The slice resource allocation problem can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization (e.g., a Virtual Network Embedding for mapping virtual nodes/links to physical resources), which is NP-hard [7]. In practice, planners have used methods like mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) to find optimal allocations, or simpler heuristics and meta-heuristics (greedy algorithms, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, etc.) to find good feasible solutions within reasonable time. Meta-heuristic approaches have been advocated because they can escape local optima and adapt the search to complex, large-scale network scenarios [7]. These techniques can incorporate QoS constraints into the objective or as hard constraints, aiming to meet slice demands while avoiding over-provisioning. 

Rule-based resource partitioning is another common traditional strategy – for example, statically dividing bandwidth or computational capacity among slices based on expected peak demands or fixed proportions. Such static slicing is straightforward and ensures isolation, but it tends to be *inefficient* and prone to QoS degradation if traffic deviates from the forecast, since the allocation cannot adapt in real time [2] [2]. In other cases, admission control and resource reservation are done conservatively: slices are over-provisioned to handle worst-case load, which achieves robustness at the cost of wasted capacity. Overall, traditional methods are as robust as their underlying assumptions – a well-tuned heuristic or optimization can guarantee QoS under the specific conditions it was designed for, but it may struggle when faced with unforeseen traffic patterns or network changes. Re-optimizing slice allocations on-the-fly in response to traffic changes is computationally expensive for large networks, limiting the real-time adaptability of classical approaches.

Despite these limitations, traditional methods have strengths in offering clear performance guarantees (when the model is accurate) and interpretability. Optimization models can exactly enforce QoS constraints and yield provably optimal (or bounded-suboptimal) solutions for the given input. By contrast, they lack the **learning** capability – i.e., they don’t improve automatically from data – so their performance degrades if the actual network conditions diverge from the modeled scenario. This has opened the door for AI/ML techniques that can learn complex relationships and decision policies directly from data or interactions.

In the periodic scenario, vanilla REINFORCE achieves better throughput — with a latency trade-off — and is co-located with SAC-RE on the second front." [2]

sections.text:
Machine learning-based approaches to slice management aim to automate and adapt the resource orchestration using data-driven intelligence. Broadly, ML algorithms can **analyze large volumes of network data**, detect patterns or anomalies, predict future demand, and quickly adapt decisions to changing conditions [6]. This adaptivity is crucial for modern networks where traffic loads and service mix can vary rapidly. Key AI/ML techniques explored for slicing include:

- **Predictive Analytics and Supervised Learning:** These use historical data to forecast traffic or performance indicators, and then adjust slice resources proactively. For instance, supervised models (regression, random forests, neural networks) have been used to predict slice capacity needs or user load, outpacing traditional threshold-based schemes in accuracy. By capturing nonlinear dependencies in QoS metrics, ML predictors can help allocate resources more precisely, improving efficiency. However, purely supervised solutions depend on the availability of representative training data for all scenarios; they may struggle with **generalization** if the network environment shifts beyond the training distribution (e.g., new applications or sudden flash traffic events).

- **Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Deep RL:** RL has emerged as a powerful approach for closed-loop slice resource control. In RL, an agent learns by interacting with the network environment (e.g., observing slice performance under a certain allocation decision and receiving a reward signal) and iteratively improves its policy. This model-free paradigm does not require an explicit mathematical model of the network’s behavior, which is a major advantage in high-dimensional, complex systems where writing an accurate model is infeasible [1]. Early works applied Q-learning or policy-gradient methods to dynamically allocate resources (bandwidth, CPU, spectrum) to slices based on observed state (queue lengths, throughput, etc.), aiming to maximize long-term QoS and resource utilization. **Deep** RL (DRL) incorporates neural networks to estimate value functions or policies, allowing it to handle large state-action spaces. DRL agents can autonomously find slicing strategies that adapt to time-varying traffic demand and network conditions, often outperforming static allocations in simulation studies.

- **Hybrid AI-Optimization Algorithms:** Recognizing that pure learning approaches sometimes have limitations in stability or constraint handling, recent research has proposed hybrid solutions that combine ML with traditional optimization. For example, a neural network might be trained to act as a fast approximator for an optimization algorithm’s output, or RL may be enhanced with constrained optimization techniques (e.g., a Lagrange multiplier framework to enforce QoS constraints). These methods try to get the best of both worlds: the **speed and adaptability** of ML and the **structure and guarantees** of optimization. An illustrative example is integrating deep learning with a Lagrangian optimization for radio resource slicing – the deep model learns to allocate resources quickly, while the Lagrange method ensures constraints (like total resource budgets and inter-slice isolation) are respected [4]. Such an approach was shown to be highly scalable with respect to the number of slices and able to achieve near-optimal QoS satisfaction, even across diverse slicing scenarios [4].

AI/ML-based techniques, especially RL, introduce their own challenges. Training an RL agent can be **data-intensive and time-consuming**; standard policy-gradient methods are often not sample-efficient and may converge slowly in complex, non-stationary environments [2] [5]. Moreover, naively trained ML models can overfit to specific traffic patterns or network settings, which hurts their **generalizability** (discussed more below). Nonetheless, the consensus in recent literature is that AI-driven approaches are essential for “zero-touch” network management – they enable a shift from rigid, rule-based operation to intelligent, adaptive control that can handle the complexity and dynamics of 5G/6G networks ([www.mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/2/368#:~:text=as%20highlighted%20in%20,of%20the%20network%20slice%2C%20sufficient)). Next, we compare how these AI techniques stack up against traditional methods on the key aspects of robustness, generalizability, and efficiency.

sections.text:
**Robustness** refers to maintaining stable QoS fulfillment despite fluctuations in traffic demand or other uncertain conditions. Traditional slicing methods typically handle variability either by worst-case provisioning (ensuring each slice gets enough resources for its peak load) or by periodic reoptimization. The worst-case approach is robust in the sense of avoiding QoS violation, but it is resource-inefficient. Periodic reoptimization (solving an allocation problem whenever traffic shifts) can in theory track changes, but in practice may be too slow for rapid fluctuations and can cause oscillations or transient violations in between reconfiguration points.

AI/ML approaches, especially online learning ones, tend to be more reactive and thus potentially more robust to fast-changing conditions. An RL agent continuously observes the network state at each time-step and can adjust slice resources on the fly, which allows it to respond to traffic spikes or dips more swiftly than a human-designed schedule. Moreover, because RL optimizes for long-term cumulative reward, it can learn strategies to preemptively allocate resources in anticipation of upcoming load (if it has learned traffic patterns), thus avoiding QoS degradation before it happens. In one study, a deep RL-based slice resource controller leveraged domain randomization during training to handle a wide range of traffic patterns; as a result, it was **robust against uncertain network conditions** and maintained QoS guarantees even for previously unseen traffic profiles [3]. In their evaluation, state-of-the-art non-ML algorithms suffered up to 44% QoS degradation when tested on traffic scenarios outside their design set, whereas the RL agent kept QoS degradation below 10% on those same unseen scenarios by dynamically scaling resources [3]. This highlights the adaptive robustness of the learning-based approach – it did not rely on a fixed traffic model, but learned a policy that generalizes within the range of variability it was trained for.

However, robustness of AI methods is not automatic – it greatly depends on the training diversity and algorithm design. If an ML model is trained only on a narrow range of conditions, it may perform well there but fail catastrophically when conditions diverge (a failure of robustness). Also, some heuristic-based approaches can be inherently robust in a broad sense. For example, a simple **rule-based** policy like uniformly splitting resources among slices might seem crude, yet it provides a stable performance baseline across many situations. Rosales *et al.* (2025) compared such a uniform slicing heuristic to advanced RL and even a generative AI policy in a Wi-Fi slicing context [2] [2]. They found that the **uniform policy** was remarkably robust: in scenarios with random traffic variations, it achieved a Pareto-optimal trade-off between total throughput and latency, effectively matching or outperforming more complex RL policies on those metrics [2]. The RL agent had higher adaptability but also more variability, whereas the simplistic uniform split, while not optimizing for any particular moment, avoided severe worst-case performance drops. This suggests that traditional methods can still hold their ground in terms of robustness if they are designed conservatively. Indeed, the uniform strategy guaranteed a form of fairness and isolation (each slice always had a fixed share), preventing extreme outcomes. 

A nuanced observation is that AI and traditional strategies often approach robustness from opposite directions: traditional methods embed robustness through conservative design (allocate extra margins, simplify decisions to avoid corner cases), whereas ML methods seek to *learn* robustness from experience. The latter can yield more efficient use of resources under most conditions, but there’s a risk of failing in unmodeled extremes. To mitigate that, researchers have started incorporating safety mechanisms in learning (like conservative exploration or worst-case aware training) to combine adaptivity with reliability. For instance, constrained or risk-sensitive RL algorithms ensure that policies respect QoS constraints with high probability, making them more robust to outlier events. These advanced ML techniques align with the stringent reliability demands (e.g., URLLC) that were traditionally handled by static over-provisioning.

In summary, AI-based slice management generally improves robustness to typical traffic volatility, by continuously adjusting allocations based on real-time feedback. Yet, truly **worst-case** robustness (guaranteeing QoS under any imaginable surge) may still require either extremely well-trained agents or complementary rule-based safeguards. A combination of approaches – using ML for agility and classical methods for hard safety bounds – is a promising direction to ensure robustness under all conditions.

sections.text:
**Generalizability** refers to how well an approach performs when facing scenarios, configurations, or traffic patterns that were not explicitly tuned or seen in development. It is closely related to adaptability: a generalizable solution can be deployed in new contexts (different slice mixes, network topologies, etc.) with minimal reconfiguration and still perform effectively. 

Traditional optimization methods are grounded in mathematical models and do not involve a training process per se, so in one sense they are general by design: an optimal resource allocation formulation can be applied to any input instance of that formulated problem. For example, if one formulates a slice allocation linear program for a given network, it can in principle handle any combination of input demands (making it “general” within that problem’s scope). However, this comes with caveats. If the model’s assumptions change – say a new type of QoS metric is introduced, or dependencies like interference in wireless slices that were neglected become significant – the traditional solution does not automatically adapt; it requires reformulating the model or tuning new heuristic rules. In other words, classical methods are as general as the fidelity of their model of reality. They may not cope well with paradigm shifts (for instance, moving from a wired-core slicing scenario to one that includes wireless RAN slicing with time-varying channels might break a model that assumed fixed link capacity).

AI/ML-based approaches often aim to be more general by training on varied data. In practice, though, many learned models **overfit** to their training conditions. A prominent challenge noted in the literature is that deep learning models for network slicing can have **limited generalization and adaptability** to dynamic or previously unseen slice configurations [4]. For instance, a deep neural network policy trained for a fixed number of slices or particular traffic distributions might not scale or give good results if the number of slices increases or if a new application with very different traffic characteristics comes along. Standard deep learning tends to interpolate within the domain of training data; anything outside that domain can lead to unpredictable behavior. Reinforcement learning agents also can over-specialize to the training environment (especially if the environment simulator does not capture all real-world effects).

To improve generalizability, researchers are exploring several strategies. One is **training with diversity** – using techniques like domain randomization, where the training environment parameters (traffic patterns, channel conditions, etc.) are varied widely and randomly during learning [3]. The idea is to prevent the model from relying on any one narrow pattern, thus teaching it a policy that works across a spectrum of conditions. The “risk-constrained” DRL agent by Sulaiman *et al.* (2023) is a case in point: by training on a regression model of the network and randomizing that model’s conditions, their agent learned to handle different real-world traffic patterns and QoS metrics without retraining [3]. The result was a policy that generalized well enough to keep QoS within 10% of target for new traffic scenarios, whereas other methods failed when generalizing [3].

Another approach to enhance generalizability is **hybrid/transfer learning**. As noted, Hu *et al.* (2024) propose combining constrained optimization methods with deep learning to achieve *strong generalization* beyond the training set [4]. In their framework, the structure from optimization (e.g., Lagrange multipliers capturing constraints) helps guide the learning so the solution is not purely memorizing data points but following general principles. Their neural-assisted algorithm was shown to gracefully handle varying numbers of slices and different slice configurations – a level of flexibility that pure deep learning struggled with [4]. Moreover, techniques like meta-learning or few-shot learning could allow an AI agent to quickly adapt to new scenarios by leveraging knowledge from similar tasks (e.g., adapting a slicing policy trained on one network to a slightly different network using only a small amount of additional training data).

On the flip side, one should note that some *traditional* strategies can be quite general in a pragmatic sense. For instance, a meta-heuristic algorithm (like an evolutionary algorithm for slice embedding) doesn’t “train” on specific traffic data; it solves each new instance from scratch via iterative improvement. This means it will attempt to solve any instance of the problem, even ones that look very different from past ones, making it generally applicable. The downside is it may need more computation time for each new instance and might not leverage experience from past instances. In contrast, an ML model expends a lot of computation in training upfront, with the payoff being fast decisions later – but if the new instance is outside its learned experience, that training effort doesn’t guarantee a good solution. Thus, generalizability is a key dimension where traditional and ML methods differ: model-based methods generalize through problem formulation (but need re-formulation for new problem types), whereas ML methods generalize through training data (and need retraining or adaptation for novel contexts). 

The latest research shows a trend toward **improving ML generalization** to make AI-driven slicing viable in the wild. We see efforts like federated learning (to train models on a wider range of conditions drawn from multiple deployments), continual learning (so the model can keep learning after deployment to adjust to evolving conditions), and robust training (e.g., adversarial training to not be thrown off by anomalous inputs). With these, AI-based methods are steadily closing the gap, aiming to be as general and reliable as the well-understood traditional algorithms, while surpassing them in adaptability.

sections.text:
Efficiency in end-to-end slice management can be interpreted in two ways: **(1)** how efficiently the approach utilizes resources to meet QoS (i.e., avoiding both over-provisioning and under-provisioning), and **(2)** the computational and operational efficiency (can the solution scale to large networks and run in real-time?). Both aspects are crucial: network operators want to maximize resource usage (since unused capacity is lost revenue) and need algorithms that can make decisions quickly as network conditions change or as the network grows.

From a resource utilization standpoint, AI/ML techniques have shown notable advantages. By learning from data or direct interactions, they can often find non-intuitive allocation patterns that yield higher overall performance. For example, an RL agent might learn to temporarily throttle one slice slightly (still within its SLA) if it predicts that another slice will have a short burst that is more critical – something a static algorithm might not allow. This dynamic resource **sharing** can improve efficiency. In quantitative terms, the DRL agent in [3] was able to minimize allocated resources while keeping QoS within acceptable bounds, whereas a static approach either wasted resources (when provisioned for worst-case) or violated QoS (when tuned for average-case) on unseen traffic [3]. The learning-based approach essentially achieved a better balance, adjusting allocation in real time to exactly what was needed. Similarly, supervised learning models that predict demand can prevent overallocation by forecasting more accurately than human-set margins. As networks become more complex (with hundreds of slices and highly variable demands), these automated approaches to squeeze out extra efficiency become increasingly valuable.

On the other hand, **computational efficiency** and scalability remain considerations. Traditional optimization solvers (like MILP solvers) can find optimal solutions for slicing in small-to-medium sized scenarios, but they may not scale to large networks with many slices and nodes due to NP-hard complexity [7]. Heuristic algorithms are faster but often problem-specific; as the scenario size grows or changes, one might need to fine-tune or redesign the heuristic. ML methods invert this: the heavy lifting is during the training phase. Training a deep RL agent or a deep neural network can be computationally intensive and might require simulators, especially if a lot of data (or exploration of environment) is needed. However, once trained, the policy execution (a forward pass through a neural network) is typically very fast – decisions can be made in milliseconds, enabling real-time control. This makes the *run-time* efficiency of ML solutions very high, suitable for online adaptation, provided the model is already trained. 

A potential concern is how training time scales with problem size. If one needs to retrain an RL agent from scratch every time the network scale increases or a new slice type is introduced, that could become a bottleneck. Researchers are addressing this by designing **scalable learning frameworks**. For instance, the neural Lagrangian method by Hu *et al.* can accommodate varying numbers of slices without retraining, demonstrating scalability in problem size [4]. Also, **online learning** algorithms (like multi-armed bandits or online convex optimization) have been proposed to adjust slicing in nearly real-time without heavy offline training; these algorithms (e.g., EXP3 or other bandit algorithms) update decisions on the fly and have theoretical performance guarantees in terms of regret. A recent work comparing an online learning approach (EXP3) and a deep RL (DQN) for AI service slicing showed each has strengths: the bandit method quickly adapts to changing conditions with low overhead, while the DQN, after sufficient training, can achieve higher longer-term performance but needs more samples to get there ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03686#:~:text=integrating%20the%20two%20concepts%20of,touch%20network%20capabilities)) ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03686#:~:text=Exploration%20and%20Exploitation%20,touch%20network%20capabilities)). Such findings suggest a trade-off: simple online algorithms vs. more complex deep RL – the former might be more efficient to deploy, while the latter can yield better absolute performance if given enough time.

**Scalability** also pertains to how solutions cope with the multi-domain nature of end-to-end slicing (RAN, transport, core). Traditional approaches often decompose the problem (optimize RAN slicing separately from core slicing, etc.), which can limit global optimality. ML approaches, especially end-to-end deep learning, can potentially handle a higher-dimensional joint optimization (for example, allocate radio, networking, and edge computing resources in one framework). This holistic view can improve efficiency by trading off resources across domains. But training such an end-to-end model is computationally challenging and poses scalability issues in terms of state/action space explosion [2]. Work is ongoing on hierarchical or distributed RL to tackle this (multiple agents managing parts of the network and coordinating). Meanwhile, hierarchical optimization (a traditional method where each domain is managed with some reserved margins) is simpler but may leave some efficiency on the table due to suboptimal domain interaction.

In summary, AI/ML-based techniques tend to offer **better resource efficiency** through fine-grained adaptation and predictive allocation, whereas traditional methods may either over-provision (wasting resources) or require solving complex optimizations repeatedly (computationally intensive) to avoid QoS loss. In terms of computational efficiency, once deployed, ML policies can act very fast and scale to frequent decision-making, but their development incurs a training cost and complexity. Traditional methods are easier to configure initially (no training needed, just solve or follow heuristic), but might not be fast enough for large problem instances or rapid reconfigurations. The choice often comes down to the operational scenario: for relatively static slice configurations, an optimization or heuristic might be sufficient and simpler; for highly dynamic situations, the investment in ML can pay off by keeping the network running near optimal efficiency most of the time.

sections.text:
AI/ML-based optimization techniques are transforming end-to-end slice management by introducing learning and adaptability into a domain historically managed by static, human-designed algorithms. Compared to traditional methods, ML approaches generally excel in **robustness** to typical traffic variability and **efficiency** of resource usage, as they can preempt and react to changes swiftly and allocate resources with fine granularity. They also automate the decision process, which is crucial for zero-touch network slicing in 5G/6G. Traditional methods, however, still hold strengths in **predictable behavior** and guaranteed compliance within their design scope, which often translates to dependable (if sometimes over-conservative) robustness and straightforward generalizability within modeled scenarios. The key weakness of purely traditional solutions is their inflexibility – they struggle to generalize or remain efficient when confronted with conditions outside their initial assumptions, whereas ML solutions are designed to learn these new conditions (given data or experience).

That said, current research indicates that a **fusion of approaches** may yield the best results. Hybrid models that leverage the reliability of optimization theory and the adaptability of machine learning are emerging to address the shortcomings of each in isolation [4] [4]. For instance, using ML to rapidly approximate an optimal solution and then fine-tuning it with a few optimization steps can provide both speed and accuracy. On the other hand, incorporating safety rules or constraint checks into an RL agent can prevent it from taking aberrant actions, marrying robustness with flexibility.

In evaluating robustness, generalizability, and efficiency, one should also consider the specific context: a solution that is “robust” in a lab setting might falter in a real network if it hasn’t been exposed to certain failure modes (raising the importance of extensive training and testing for ML approaches). Likewise, a “general” traditional algorithm might theoretically apply to any scenario but yield suboptimal results everywhere unless carefully re-tuned for each scenario. Therefore, ongoing work often benchmarks AI/ML methods against traditional baselines across many metrics and scenarios. Contradictory findings in literature – such as an RL method outperforming a heuristic in one study, while a simple rule performs nearly as well as RL in another – usually can be attributed to differences in assumptions and conditions. It underscores that no one method is universally best; robust slice management likely requires a toolkit of methods.

In conclusion, AI/ML-based techniques offer a promising path to handle the complexity of end-to-end slice management under variable traffic and strict QoS demands, showing clear advantages in adaptivity and often in efficiency. Traditional methods provide a valuable foundation and safety net, ensuring that known constraints are met and offering interpretable insights. The trend is toward intelligent orchestration systems that integrate learning-based modules with classical optimization, achieving a balance where network slicing is both **autonomous** and **trustworthy**. For the scientific community and network operators, the goal is to continue enhancing the **generalizability** of AI models and the **real-time robustness** of algorithms so that future networks can self-optimize reliably in the face of ever-changing requirements.

sections.text: The convergence of large language models (LLMs) with telecommunication networks is opening new possibilities for automating and optimizing **5G network orchestration**. Researchers envision that advanced generative AI models (like GPT-style LLMs) can usher in “a new era of autonomous wireless networks” where one versatile model handles many tasks, reducing the need for numerous specialized algorithms [1]. The outstanding comprehension and reasoning capabilities of LLMs offer a foundation to automate many telecommunication operations based on human instructions [2]. This has inspired efforts to treat LLMs as **foundation models** for networking – aiming for “one model for all tasks” in network management with strong generalization across scenarios [3]. In the 5G and beyond context, such LLM-driven solutions could help manage the increasing complexity of network slicing, resource allocation, and service optimization in a more flexible and intelligent manner.

sections.text: Early explorations and surveys highlight a broad spectrum of potential applications of LLMs in telecom. They range from generating configurations and code, to classifying network traffic or security events, to optimizing network parameters and predicting service performance [2]. The ultimate goal is an **Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)-enabled** 6G/5G network that is self-evolving and self-optimizing [2]. Achieving this vision requires overcoming significant challenges (discussed later), but recent research has made tangible progress. Below, we survey several key themes in current literature where LLMs are being applied for 5G network orchestration and management, including intent-driven network slicing, orchestration frameworks, multi-agent and hybrid AI approaches, edge-cloud coordination, and automated network configuration. We also discuss common challenges and emerging solutions across these works.

sections.text: One of the prominent use cases for LLMs in telecom is **intent-based network slicing orchestration**. In 5G, network slicing allows operators to create customized virtual network slices with specific Quality of Service (QoS) for different applications – but orchestrating these slices is complex, especially across multiple domains. Recent research proposes leveraging LLMs to bridge the gap between a user’s high-level service requests and the low-level slice configuration. For example, Yaacoub *et al.* (2024) describe a framework where an LLM serves as an intent parser within a network slicing management system [4]. When an enterprise or customer describes their needs in natural language (e.g. *"require ultra-reliable low-latency connectivity for an automation system"*), the LLM-based agent translates this intent into the technical requirements and parameters for a network slice [4]. Specifically, the LLM can map the requested service levels to the necessary network functions and resources on the infrastructure, effectively automating what would normally be a human-driven configuration process [4]. This approach simplifies the interaction between end-users and the 5G orchestration system, allowing customers to request slices in plain language while the LLM handles the complexity of interpreting and fulfilling those requests.

sections.text: To handle the end-to-end slice lifecycle, the intent-parsing LLM is complemented by other agents in a multi-agent system [4]. In the proposed framework, the **LLM agent** parses user intent and formulates the slice deployment plan, which is then coordinated with existing Management and Orchestration (MANO) platforms (such as ETSI/3GPP management frameworks). Meanwhile, additional specialized agents manage domain-specific tasks or enforce policies across different administrative domains [4]. This hierarchical multi-agent setup ensures that, once the LLM converts the user’s request into a slice template, the rest of the orchestration (instantiating virtual network functions, allocating resources, etc.) can be carried out automatically across possibly multiple operators or technology domains. The LLM’s robust language understanding is key to making the interface “human-friendly” without sacrificing technical accuracy. Overall, intent-based slicing research demonstrates an early successful use of LLMs to **interpret high-level objectives and turn them into orchestrated network actions** – a significant step toward zero-touch network management in 5G.

sections.text: Beyond specific slicing use-cases, researchers are crafting more general **LLM-driven orchestration frameworks** for wireless networks. A representative example is the **NetOrchLLM framework** proposed by Abdallah *et al.* (2024) [5]. NetOrchLLM is introduced as an LLM-based network orchestrator that can coordinate a variety of domain-specific models and network functions using natural language reasoning. The authors note that, until now, most discussions of LLMs in network management have been largely *visionary* – highlighting potential benefits without concrete implementations [5]. NetOrchLLM attempts to fill this gap by providing a practical design and prototype for incorporating an LLM into the network control loop. In this framework, the LLM acts as a high-level decision-making engine that can invoke or interact with wireless network models (for tasks like traffic prediction, routing optimization, interference management, etc.), essentially using language as the “glue” to orchestrate these components [5].

sections.text: The NetOrchLLM framework demonstrates how an LLM’s broad knowledge and reasoning ability can improve network operations. For instance, given a dense heterogeneous network scenario, the LLM can gather insights (from prompts or telemetry described in text) and then generate commands or configurations to optimize performance metrics [5]. It was shown to manage dynamic environments and improve overall network performance by making more holistic decisions, rather than siloed optimizations per individual model [5]. This indicates that LLMs might serve as “meta-controllers” that consider a wider context (including learned knowledge from training data) when orchestrating network behaviors. By bridging the gap between high-level intent and low-level model actions, NetOrchLLM and similar efforts **pave the way for integrating generative AI into real network management loops**. They also highlight new research issues like how to represent network state in language form and how to ensure the LLM’s decisions are reliable. Nonetheless, the early results are promising: LLM-based frameworks can indeed handle complex wireless scenarios and yield performance gains, pointing to a future where LLMs augment traditional network control algorithms.

sections.text: While a single LLM can handle language understanding, combining it with other specialized agents can significantly enhance orchestration in complex networks. **Multi-agent systems augmented by LLMs** have been proposed as a solution to overcome some limitations of applying vanilla LLMs to network management. A prime example is the work by Jiang *et al.* (2023) on *LLM-enhanced multi-agent systems for 6G communications* [6][6]. This approach acknowledges that directly deploying an off-the-shelf LLM in a network environment faces challenges – for instance, an LLM alone may lack up-to-date domain knowledge of proprietary network data, or could struggle with reasoning about dynamic network states [6]. To address these gaps, the authors integrate the LLM into a **multi-agent framework** where it cooperates with purpose-built agents endowed with tools like domain-specific data retrieval, problem planning, and solution evaluation capabilities [6].

sections.text: In the referenced 6G multi-agent system, the LLM essentially plays the role of a global coordinator and reasoning engine, while other agents supply it with facts and check its outputs. The framework defines multiple agent components: (1) a **data retrieval agent** that can query and summarize telecom knowledge bases or live network data for the LLM [6], (2) a **collaborative planning agent** (or set of agents) that uses the LLM’s outputs to draft feasible network control plans from different perspectives [6], and (3) an **evaluation/refinement agent** that assesses the LLM’s proposed solutions and prompts it to refine them if needed [6]. By distributing these responsibilities, the system capitalizes on the LLM’s strengths (flexible reasoning and understanding of intent) while compensating for its weaknesses (factual accuracy and domain depth) through specialized modules. Initial case studies, such as a semantic communication optimization, have validated this design – the LLM-driven agent team was able to solve a network problem specified in natural language by retrieving relevant technical knowledge and iteratively improving the solution [6][6]. Such multi-agent strategies point toward a **cognitive network orchestrator** that is greater than the sum of its parts: the LLM provides general intelligence and intent parsing, and the surrounding agents ensure domain correctness, safety, and up-to-date information. This line of research is expected to grow, as it offers a practical path to embed LLMs into networks without relying on the LLM alone for every detail.

sections.text: Another recurring theme is the integration of LLMs with **reinforcement learning (RL)** and other closed-loop control techniques to handle dynamic network orchestration. The rationale is that LLMs excel at high-level reasoning and planning, but may not be well-suited for fast, fine-grained control updates – whereas RL agents can learn optimal actions through trial-and-error in a specific environment. By combining the two, researchers aim to get the best of both worlds. For example, Shokrnezhad and Taleb (2025) propose an autonomous orchestration framework called *ARC* for beyond-5G/6G networks that uses LLMs for **high-level decision-making** and RL for low-level, continuous adaptation [10]. In their design, the LLM (augmented with a retrieval module for domain knowledge) monitors the network’s state and generates *strategic plans* or recommendations using chain-of-thought reasoning [10]. These high-level plans could include decisions like how to route traffic during congestion or how to reallocate resources when a new service comes online. Then, a hierarchy of RL agents (operating as a *Hierarchical Action Planner*) takes those plans and executes them in the network environment, handling the real-time decisions and fine-tuning the actions to the current conditions [10]. Essentially, the orchestration is **decomposed into two tiers**: the LLM plans “what to do” in a broad sense, and the RL agents figure out “how to do it” optimally at the granular level. This method showed improved efficiency and adaptability in simulations of a complex network, because the LLM’s global guidance helped the RL converge on better policies faster [11].

sections.text: A similar hybrid approach has been applied to the **Open RAN (O-RAN)** architecture in 5G networks. O-RAN splits RAN control into a non-real-time (non-RT) layer and a near-real-time (near-RT) layer. Bao *et al.* (2025) introduced an *LLM-empowered hierarchical RIC* (Radio Intelligent Controller) framework, dubbed **LLM-hRIC**, in which an LLM operates at the non-RT RIC and conventional AI (like RL) operates at the near-RT RIC [11]. In LLM-hRIC, the large language model is deployed as a **rApp (resident app)** in the non-real-time controller to provide strategic guidance and policy – for instance, formulating an initial resource allocation plan or optimizing long-term parameters based on large-scale network data [11]. Meanwhile, a reinforcement learning based xApp runs in the near-real-time controller, handling immediate RAN control loops (which require decisions on the order of milliseconds to seconds). The LLM and RL agents cooperate: the LLM’s output serves as a strong prior or high-level policy for the RL, and the RL fine-tunes it to actual radio environment conditions [11][11]. In power allocation use-case experiments, this hierarchical LLM+RL control achieved higher network throughput than baseline approaches, thanks to the *“high-quality initial policies, generated by the LLM, which enhance exploration efficiency”* for the RL agent [11]. These results underscore that **LLMs can significantly boost learning-based network control** by injecting expert knowledge and long-horizon planning into the loop. However, by offloading time-critical decisions to simpler agents, the overall system remains responsive. As 5G networks evolve, such hierarchical AI controllers could help meet real-time performance requirements while still leveraging the intelligence of LLMs at an upper layer.

sections.text: Implementing an LLM for network orchestration doesn’t necessarily mean running a giant model centrally; another line of research explores **distributed, edge-cloud collaborative frameworks**. The motivation is that 5G networks often have computing capabilities at the edge (base stations, edge data centers) which can host AI functions closer to users, reducing latency and allowing localization of knowledge. Chen *et al.* (2023) put forward **NetGPT**, an *“AI-native” network architecture*, which splits LLM workloads between edge and cloud in a coordinated way [8][8]. In NetGPT, smaller LLM instances (or specially fine-tuned models) reside at the network edge to handle personalized and context-aware tasks – for example, inferring user intent or local network conditions from prompts – while larger LLMs at the cloud core handle more computationally intensive reasoning and maintain a global view [8][8]. The edge LLMs can utilize real-time, location-specific information (such as local traffic patterns or user preferences), which they incorporate into prompts or partial solutions that are sent to the central LLM. This division of labor not only improves latency (because the edge LLM can quickly respond to local events), but also can make the overall orchestration more scalable and privacy-friendly (since raw data can be processed at the edge).

sections.text: NetGPT’s design emphasizes a deep integration of communication and computing, reflecting a **“native AI” approach to network architecture** [8]. One key insight is that the predictive and intent-understanding capabilities of edge LLMs can serve as a *unified solution for intelligent network management and orchestration* at the user-facing side [8]. For instance, an edge LLM might predict a surge in video traffic in a cell based on trending content (a form of popularity prediction) and pre-emptively signal the cloud orchestrator to allocate more bandwidth or edge caching for that service [8]. The cloud LLM, receiving such inputs from many edge nodes, can aggregate and optimize resource provisioning network-wide. In the demonstration, the authors fine-tuned open-source LLMs (GPT-2 and LLaMA models) for edge and core roles, and showed that this collaboration outperformed strategies that rely purely on cloud processing or only local models [8]. As 5G moves towards 6G, such **edge-cloud LLM synergies** could become important for handling massive distributed intelligence – allowing networks to personalize services and orchestrate resources in real-time, all through the natural interface of language-like commands and knowledge sharing between AI agents.

sections.text: Network orchestration often boils down to configuring a multitude of devices and services – a task that is notoriously complex and error-prone when done manually. Here, LLMs have shown great potential in **automating network configuration** and making network management more accessible. One compelling example is **NetBuddy**, a system by Wang *et al.* (2024) that uses LLMs (specifically GPT-4 in their prototype) to translate high-level policies into low-level network configurations [9]. The idea is to enable network operators to simply describe what they need in plain language or high-level objectives, and let the LLM generate the required router/switch configuration commands or even code (e.g., P4 programs for software-defined switches, BGP routing configurations, etc.) [9]. NetBuddy tackles this by breaking down configuration generation into granular steps and employing *self-healing code generation*, meaning the LLM iteratively refines its outputs (possibly by re-checking or testing them in an emulator) to ensure they are syntactically and semantically correct [9]. In a proof-of-concept, the authors showed GPT-4 could successfully convert a set of natural language requirements into a working P4 datapath program and BGP settings, which then ran in a network emulator to validate connectivity [9].

sections.text: The broader implication of such work is that **LLMs can serve as highly intelligent assistants for network operators**. They not only automate configuration synthesis but can also help with tasks like detecting misconfigurations or suggesting fixes. (Indeed, other studies have shown that off-the-shelf LLMs can identify configuration errors or policy violations in network setups by reasoning about the config as text, though care must be taken to validate LLM suggestions ([ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.09690#:~:text=Models%20ar5iv,and%20false%20positives%20that%20require)).) By minimizing human involvement in routine configuration, these tools reduce the risk of outages caused by mistakes and free up engineers to focus on higher-level design. In addition, LLMs can generate documentation or explanations alongside configurations, helping human operators understand the changes – effectively bridging the gap between intent and implementation. This trend aligns with the vision of **self-driving networks**, where the network can reconfigure itself on the fly based on operator intents or autonomously in response to events, with LLMs providing the natural language interface and cognitive engine to do so. While currently such LLM-driven configuration is at an early stage, it’s rapidly improving, and we can anticipate future 5G/6G management systems where much of the heavy lifting of writing and verifying configuration code is handled by an LLM (with oversight), speeding up deployment and reducing errors.

sections.text: Despite the encouraging progress, using LLMs for 5G network orchestration comes with a set of **challenges and open issues** that researchers are actively addressing. A fundamental concern is the reliability and correctness of LLM outputs. By nature, LLMs can produce *plausible-sounding but incorrect* statements – a phenomenon known as hallucination. In a network context, an LLM “hallucinating” a faulty configuration or an invalid optimization could have serious consequences. Indeed, Shokrnezhad *et al.* note that early solutions integrating LLMs into network control **had not sufficiently tackled LLM hallucinations or adaptation to network dynamics** [10]. Ensuring factual accuracy and consistency with real network states is difficult because most LLMs are trained on general text and lack exposure to live network telemetry. To mitigate this, many works introduce retrieval or grounding mechanisms (as described above) so that the LLM’s decisions are informed by up-to-date network data or domain knowledge bases [6][10]. Another reliability strategy is to keep an LLM “in the loop” in a high-level capacity while a deterministic or learning-based controller (like an RL agent) verifies or fine-tunes the decisions, as seen in the hierarchical frameworks (ARC, LLM-hRIC) that mix LLM planning with robust lower-layer control [10][11].

sections.text: **Scalability and deployment feasibility** of LLMs in operational networks is another challenge. Large models can be computationally intensive and may not meet real-time processing requirements of certain network functions (for example, a base station scheduling decisions every few milliseconds). This is why researchers are exploring model compression, distillation, and edge deployment of smaller LLMs [2]. There is ongoing work on specialized telecom LLMs that are smaller and more efficient, or techniques to offload heavy computations to cloud while keeping latency-sensitive decisions local (as in NetGPT). Data privacy and security are also key considerations. Telecom networks deal with sensitive customer data and critical infrastructure, so any AI component needs to ensure data is handled securely. Incorporating an LLM raises questions about how to prevent leakage of private information and how to guard against adversarial inputs or **“network prompt injections”** that could manipulate the model. Recent surveys list issues like *data availability, computational power, security backdoors, trust, validation, interoperability,* and privacy as hurdles for LLM adoption in telecom [4]. Addressing these will likely involve industry-wide standards (for model auditing, safe deployment practices) and technical innovations (like fine-tuning LLMs on telecom data with differential privacy, or adding explainability and verification modules around the LLM).

sections.text: In summary, the use of LLMs for 5G network orchestration is a rapidly evolving field. The **contrasting claims** in the literature – from optimistic visions of one-model-for-all-network-tasks [1] to cautious notes on current limitations [10] – are being reconciled through active research. Techniques such as multi-agent augmentation, hybrid LLM+RL control, and edge-cloud splitting are forming a toolkit to overcome LLMs’ drawbacks while leveraging their strengths. Over the next few years, we can expect more **real-world trials** of LLM-based orchestration in telecom, and possibly the first deployments in areas like automated network slicing or customer service chatbots configuring network services on the fly. The consensus in the community is that LLMs (and generative AI at large) will become an integral part of network automation pipelines [1][5], provided we continue to refine their reliability, efficiency, and alignment with domain requirements. Such efforts will eventually pave the way for intelligent, self-driven 6G networks that can understand objectives, reason about complex trade-offs, and orchestrate network resources autonomously – fulfilling the promise of AI-powered network orchestration that current 5G networks are just beginning to explore.

question: What approaches can be utilized to model the end-to-end response time of a virtual network function, accounting for processing latency and queuing delays under dynamic traffic conditions?

sections.text: One common approach to model the end-to-end response time of a Virtual Network Function (VNF) is through **queueing theory**. In such models, each VNF (or each processing component of it) is treated as a server queue that packets must pass through, incurring **processing latency** (service time) and **queuing delay** (waiting time if the server is busy). Under dynamic traffic (where arrival rates fluctuate or are stochastic), queueing models can capture how varying load impacts the response time. A simple example is an M/M/1 queue (Poisson arrivals, exponential service) representing a single VNF instance. *Fahmin et al.* used an M/M/1 model to analyze an NFV system and found that analytical results matched simulation, demonstrating the viability of Markovian queues for NFV performance modeling [3]. In general, an M/M/1 queue’s mean response time is given by $1/(μ-λ)$ (for arrival rate $λ$ and service rate $μ$), illustrating how higher load $λ$ drives up latency. Such basic models provide intuition, though real VNFs often have non-Poisson traffic and non-exponential service times that require more advanced models.To handle **general traffic patterns and service distributions** (e.g. bursty arrivals or heavy-tailed processing times), researchers resort to *M/G/1* or *G/G/1* queues and **open queueing networks** comprised of multiple queues. These are analytically intractable in closed-form, so approximate methods and numerical analysis are used. For example, *Prados-Garzón et al.* developed an **open queueing network** model with general distributions (modeled as G/G/m queues for multi-core VNFs) to evaluate the response time of a virtualized service [2]. They solved the model with techniques like the **Queueing Network Analyzer (QNA)** and **Mean Value Analysis (MVA)**, which approximate the average delays in each queue. Notably, their model was validated on a testbed with a virtualized Mobility Management Entity (vMME) VNF, and it accurately predicted the mean response time under various loads [2]. The QNA method yielded latency estimates with less than half the error of simpler analytical techniques at medium/high workloads (where system dynamics are complex) [2]. This demonstrates that queueing-network models, calibrated with appropriate parameters, can capture the processing and queuing behavior of VNFs even under **dynamic traffic conditions**. Such models are useful for what-if analysis; for instance, they can support **resource dimensioning** – determining how much CPU or memory a VNF needs to meet latency targets under a given traffic load [2].When a service consists of a **chain of VNFs** (a service function chain), the end-to-end response time accumulates the processing and queuing delays at each VNF in sequence. Analytical models in this case consider a **tandem queueing network**. A straightforward approach might assume each VNF sees a Poisson input (e.g. using a Jackson network model), but in reality the departure process from one VNF can be bursty or correlated, violating Jackson assumptions (making the network **non-product-form**). Researchers address this by **decomposition and approximation** techniques. *Ye et al.* proposed an end-to-end **delay modeling framework** for VNF chains that accounted for both processing and link queuing at each hop [1] [1]. They introduced a **dominant-resource generalized processor sharing (DR-GPS)** scheduler to fairly allocate processing (CPU) and transmission (bandwidth) resources among flows sharing a VNF, ensuring that each packet sees at most one bottleneck at a time [1]. This allowed them to **decouple the queueing** at the CPU and NIC: essentially, by allocating just enough bandwidth to match each flow’s processed output rate, they eliminated queuing on the output link, leaving only a single queue (CPU queue) per VNF. Each VNF in the chain could then be modeled as an **M/D/1** queue (Poisson arrivals, deterministic service equal to the allocated share) in their approximation [1]. The authors showed that this approach produces a **tighter delay bound** than a naive single-queue (e.g. G/D/1) model, especially under heavy load where inter-departure times become more regular [1]. By iterating this analysis from one VNF to the next (propagating the effective departure process as the arrival process to the next), they obtained the end-to-end response time for the chain. Notably, the model was validated via simulation: the predicted queueing delays at each stage closely matched those observed in packet-level simulations under varying traffic rates [1]. This indicates that careful analytical modeling (with appropriate scheduling assumptions and decoupling approximations) can accurately capture **dynamic traffic effects** – for example, the model remained accurate for both lightly loaded and heavily loaded scenarios by adjusting the service share per flow [1].Other researchers have also tackled VNF chain modeling with advanced queueing methods. Some have employed **non-product-form queueing networks** with custom solution techniques. For instance, *De Simone et al.* consider a 5G core network where key nodes (VNFs like the core control-plane functions) are modeled as **G/G/m queues**, which do not have closed-form solutions. They apply a **decomposition-based analytical method** to these queues, calculating performance metrics for each node in isolation (with adjusted traffic statistics) and then iteratively refining the estimates to account for interactions in the chain [4]. This approach allows evaluating the end-to-end latency even when traffic patterns are complex and inter-node dependencies exist. Such stochastic network models capture both **processing latency and queuing** at each VNF under realistic, time-varying workloads.

Simulation results demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed E2E delay modeling framework..." [1] [1]

sections.text: While queueing theory often focuses on average or distributional response times, another approach considers **worst-case (bounded) latency** using *network calculus*. Network calculus is a theoretical framework that models traffic flows and servers with deterministically bounded arrival and service functions. It is well-suited to derive **hard upper bounds** on delay, accounting for bursty arrivals and scheduling guarantees – a relevant perspective for dynamic conditions where traffic can spike. In the context of VNFs, a network calculus model would describe each VNF (or each link+VNF combination) with a service curve (e.g. minimum service rate or latency-rate server model) and each traffic flow with an arrival curve (e.g. a token-bucket describing maximum burst and average rate). Using these, one can compute a worst-case queuing delay for the flow through that function (and concatenation of functions).Recent research has applied network calculus to VNF chains. *Wang et al.* derived **delay bounds for a chain of VNFs** using network calculus methods [6]. In their approach, the virtual network function chain is modeled similarly to a tandem of servers in series, and by composing the service curves and arrival curves, they obtained a formula for the maximum delay a packet could experience from ingress to egress of the chain. This approach intrinsically accounts for **dynamic traffic bursts**: for example, if the input traffic has a burst of a certain size, the calculus can bound the queuing delay that burst will induce given the processing rate of the VNF. An earlier example by *Yao et al.* (2013) demonstrated the use of network calculus to model delays in a **virtualized wireless network** – conceptually similar since a base station was virtualized into slices, akin to VNFs [5]. They provided a **delay model that included both the physical and virtual queueing resources** and used network calculus to compute an upper bound on packet delay through the system [5]. The results showed that the model could effectively predict delay bounds and was useful for admission control (ensuring new flows wouldn’t violate latency guarantees) [5]. The trade-off is that these network-calculus-derived bounds apply to worst-case scenarios; in many cases the actual average latency will be much lower. However, for stringent applications (e.g. 5G URLLC scenarios or industrial control systems), having a guaranteed **upper bound** on VNF response time under all traffic conditions is critical. Thus, network calculus provides a complementary approach to queueing theory: it is pessimistic but **robust to traffic variability**, making it suitable when one needs to account for *any* dynamic fluctuation in traffic (not just typical or average conditions).

sections.text: Analytical models sometimes struggle to capture the full complexity of dynamic traffic behaviors (especially if arrival processes are non-stationary or workloads shift unpredictably). In such cases, **discrete-event simulation** and empirical measurement are invaluable tools to model VNF response times. Using packet-level simulators (like *OMNeT++*, *ns-3*, or custom event-driven simulations), researchers can create a virtual network function instance and feed it time-varying traffic to observe the resulting processing and queuing delays. This approach inherently accounts for dynamic effects such as bursty arrivals, time-varying service rates (if the VNF’s processing capacity changes or if there is background load), and complex scheduling interactions that might be difficult to formulate analytically. For example, in the study by *Ye et al.*, the authors **simulated two VNF chains in OMNeT++** to verify their analytic delay model [1]. The simulation introduced dynamic flows with different `time profiles` (processing vs transmission demand) and showed how queue lengths and delays evolved over time; the results closely matched the theoretical predictions, lending confidence that the model holds under realistic traffic dynamics [1]. Simulation not only validates models but can also directly answer performance questions when analysis is infeasible – e.g. one can simulate a VNF under a recorded real traffic trace to see its full distribution of response times.**Empirical measurement** on actual deployments or testbeds is another approach. Here, a VNF is deployed in a controlled environment (or even in production), and one measures its processing latency and queuing delay by instrumenting the system. *Prados-Garzón et al.* not only built a model but also **experimentally measured a vMME’s performance** on a data-center-like testbed to calibrate and validate their queueing network model [2]. By doing so, they ensured that real-world factors such as virtualization overhead, CPU scheduling delays from the hypervisor, and background load interference were accounted for in the model’s parameters. Empirical data can reveal, for instance, if service times have high variance or if there are periodic bursts in arrival traffic – information that can refine analytical assumptions (e.g. choosing G/G/m over M/M/1). Moreover, empirical modeling can capture **non-stationary behavior** (such as diurnal load patterns or sudden surges) by replaying or extrapolating from measured traces. When combined with analytical insights, empirical approaches can guide **dynamic provisioning** strategies – for example, using a model to decide when to scale out a VNF instance in anticipation of a traffic spike. In fact, the aforementioned performance model by Prados-Garzón was suggested as a tool for **dynamic resource provisioning**, adjusting VNF resources on-the-fly to maintain low response times as the workload changes [2].In summary, **multiple approaches** exist to model end-to-end VNF response time under dynamic traffic. Queueing theory provides a rich toolkit to derive average (and sometimes distributional) delay estimates accounting for processing and queuing at one or multiple stages of a service. These models can be made more realistic via techniques like state-space decomposition, multi-resource scheduling (for CPU vs network sharing), and open-network analysis, and they have been validated against real systems. For worst-case scenarios, network calculus offers a way to bound delays even in highly variable traffic conditions, which is useful for guaranteeing QoS in critical applications. Finally, simulation and measurements serve both to validate models and to directly observe VNF performance under dynamic workloads, capturing behaviors that theoretical models might miss. By combining these approaches – analytical modeling for insight and generality, and simulation/measurement for fidelity – researchers and engineers can thoroughly understand and predict a VNF’s end-to-end response time across the full spectrum of traffic conditions, from typical loads to extreme bursts.
